It further describes front and rear suspension components and mounting features (A-arms, anti-roll bars, damping members), steering linkages and steering column/gear selector/tilt assembly, floorboard water-management features and traction features, and seating-base and seatback mechanisms for stowing and returning to upright positions.

The passage describes an effort by universities, including MIT, to make some master’s degrees more affordable through an online credential called a MicroMasters. MIT says the class of 2018 could save tens of thousands on a master’s in supply chain management, with MIT noting a normal cost of over $67,000 for the academic year. The MicroMasters is an online program with courses such as entrepreneurship, user interface design, and artificial intelligence offered by several universities. A case example is Danaka Porter, who says the certification costs $1,350 versus $67,938 for the full year’s master’s tuition, and that the coursework is rigorous though challenging for those without relevant backgrounds. The passage also notes that MicroMasters skills may make graduates more attractive to employers, and that companies such as GE, Walmart, IBM, and Volvo recognize MicroMasters. For schools, the passage says online course performance is considered in admissions for MIT’s blended program, which requires an additional on-campus semester at full cost to complete a graduate degree. MIT expects to admit about 40 students per year and frames admissions as more informative than relying on grades and recommendation letters alone.

The speaker discusses the urgency of an upcoming game and expects it to be exciting. They say fans have provided strong support, and they wanted to return the game in front of these fans. The speaker recalls time together during the Olympics, and that after returning they talked about playing together again; when a trade happened, it benefited the Avalanche. They credit Ray with providing leadership, raising team expectations, and showing that a hard-working, good approach to the game helps both young and older players, describing him as unselfish and focused on playing together.

The speaker says they did not lose the game last night because of goaltending and states there is zero chance that Kris Letang will return for the series. They explain that Archie was added to the lineup to bring enthusiasm, energy, speed, and a helpful dimension, and that they are confident the team will respond and improve despite disappointment with the score. The speaker notes strong contributions from Carter Rowney and says lineup decisions are made game by game, with adjustments aimed at better balance and secondary scoring. They discuss goaltending as important and cite last night’s performance as involving solid play from Matt and a tremendous game from Pekka Rinne, while emphasizing focus on controllable factors, learning from preventable goals, and preparing for the next game with excitement.

NVIDIA RTX Blackwell architecture builds on prior NVIDIA AI technologies to enable next-generation AI-powered gaming and professional applications, aiming for higher graphical realism, interactivity, and design capabilities. It cites neural rendering and NVIDIA DLSS features (Super Resolution, Frame Generation, and Ray Reconstruction) as improving GPU performance and image quality with lower computational cost, denoising, and reconstructing details. Blackwell also introduces Neural Rendering and Neural Shading technologies to accelerate developer use of AI, including real-time generative AI rendering and simulation, dynamic terrain creation, realistic physical simulations, and conversational workflows for faster 3D design iteration. The Blackwell architecture family, including RTX Blackwell and datacenter-class GPUs, is named to honor mathematician and statistician David H. Blackwell.

Hawaiʻi is expanding free preschool options by converting private preschools to charter schools. Waikīkī Community Preschool became the first program in Hawaiʻi to transition from private to charter this year, reporting to the State Public Charter School Commission, receiving state funding, and becoming tuition-free. The charter commission says charter schools currently operate 33 preschool classrooms statewide, including six at Waikīkī Community Preschool, and Hawaiʻi aims to provide all 3- and 4-year-olds access to preschool by 2032. The state also opened additional preschool classrooms on Department of Education campuses and plans more.

Advocates and preschool leaders say charter funding can help address shortages of early educators by providing more stable state funding and teacher benefits similar to K-12 public schools. However, leaders report that charter preschool funding levels are often insufficient to cover expenses like staff, rent, and facilities, leading to budget shortfalls that require nonprofit fundraising support. The passage also notes that charter preschool teachers face stricter qualification requirements, and that small programs may find it difficult to convert without outside administrative and fundraising support. The state received only two applications to become charters earlier this year, and the article discusses ongoing state efforts to fund and build preschool classrooms on government-owned land and expand preschool space at campuses with room.

Ed Silverman, a senior writer and Pharmalot columnist at STAT, covers the pharmaceutical industry and authors the “morning” column. The passage introduces a regular feature highlighting a different person each week, and this time it notes that enGene hired Hussein Sweiti as chief medical officer; previously, he worked at Johnson & Johnson as global medical head for oncology clinical development.

The passage is a mix of news headlines and promotional content. It includes headlines such as the EU pushing climate reform for development banks, major corporate moves (e.g., Fifth Third acquiring Comerica for $10.9B, JPMorgan accelerating AI integration), and other global economic and technology updates. The main promotional section focuses on PIM Capital, presenting it as a specialist in structuring and administration of funds for emerging markets and cross-border opportunities, emphasizing flexible, locally nuanced solutions to address regulatory and currency challenges and citing its network, multi-office presence, and client expansion.

The passage discusses whether it is possible to make money day trading, stating that it is possible but not an easy way to riches and that most people are unlikely to succeed. The author shares personal trading experience from January 2002 to May 2012, including accumulated profit graphs, losing-day counts in certain years, and an analysis showing that the 1% best trading days contributed 11% of total profits over the period. The author also describes how the author’s results varied over time, including a difficult period in 2011–2012, followed by improved profitability after research and implementing new strategies. The passage claims that automated trading (“algo trading”) affects day trading and may require traders to compete with automation or adopt strategies with less impact from algos, which can involve larger drawdowns. It also summarizes a case involving Tuco Trading, which was overtaken by the SEC in March 2008 for “illegal trading,” and notes that court papers reportedly showed “quite bad” profitability numbers for traders, mostly day traders. The passage concludes that day trading requires patience, preparation, and strict discipline, and suggests starting with swing trading.

Amazon.com, Inc. filed a Form 8-K dated May 30, 2018, reporting matters voted on at its Annual Meeting of Shareholders. On May 30, 2018, directors Jeffrey P. Bezos, Tom A. Alberg, Jamie S. Gorelick, Daniel P. Huttenlocher, Judith A. McGrath, Jonathan J. Rubinstein, Thomas O. Ryder, Patricia Q. Stonesifer, and Wendell P. Weeks were elected as directors, and Ernst & Young LLP was ratified as independent auditors for the fiscal year ending December 31, 2018. The compensation of named executive officers was approved in an advisory vote. Two shareholder proposals—one regarding an independent board chair and one regarding vote-counting practices—were not approved, with voting results listed for each item. The report was signed by David A. Zapolsky on June 1, 2018.

Foreign portfolio investors showed strong interest in acquiring investment limits in corporate bonds at an auction. Against a notified amount of Rs 3,360 crore for corporate bonds, 58 bidders submitted bids totaling Rs 5,898 crore. The lowest cut-off bid by FPIs was 15.25 basis points, compared with 1.20 basis points on G-secs; the highest corporate bond bid was 25 basis points versus three basis points for G-secs. For G-secs, 37 bidders bid for Rs 7,116 crore against a notified Rs 5,481 crore. The corporate bond auction is being conducted for the second time in the fiscal year.

The passage describes the “Turnaround Tuesday effect,” which is observed from the close of Monday’s trading session until at least the close of Tuesday’s session, based on the tendency for reversals in price direction. It uses examples such as Black Monday (October 19, 1987), when the market rebounded on Tuesday and Wednesday. Backtests of a strategy in SPY report higher returns than other weekday-based approaches, with buying at the Monday close performing about twice as well as buying at the Tuesday close. The passage states the effect is not a myth and has been profitable for about 30 years, but appears to work only on weak Mondays. It also notes variations of the strategy, including buying on a weak Monday (with the close at least 1% lower than Friday’s close) and selling at Tuesday’s close, and adding filters such as Intraday Breadth Strength (IBS).

The King appointed Mr. Allen and Mr. Carter to negotiate a reciprocity agreement, signed at Washington on January 30, 1875. The treaty required Congress to ratify customs dues and a proclamation to take effect, and it entered into force on September 9, 1876. Disputes arose with Great Britain and initially with Germany over a “parity” (favored nation) clause in the Anglo-Hawaiian treaty of 1852; Mr. Carter contested Germany’s position, and the U.S. construction of the clause was agreed to substantially. A compromise on a 10% duty on British imports was proposed but withdrawn, and subsequent parliamentary discussions in Hawaii led to a ministry change and the King’s minister admitting the Government’s claim to exclusive privileges and pledging to hold the treaty accordingly. The situation prompted concern about possible U.S. actions beyond the treaty, leading Mr. Evarts to instruct Mr. Comly on August 6, 1878 to disabuse such concerns. Further interpretation disputes and issues involving potential frauds were handled through diplomatic notes. A domestic scandal led to rapid minister changes and a request to recall foreign representatives, including Mr. Comly, later rescinded after another cabinet change. The Government’s good offices were also used in suppressing liquor traffic in the Ralik Islands and in arranging a consular agent. It further supported negotiations involving Hawaii and Japan, and in 1881 Mr. Comly reported Britain’s continued efforts to benefit from the parity clause through claims pending termination of the Anglo-Hawaiian treaty.

The passage describes how the antiferromagnet Sm0.7Er0.3FeO3 is studied to understand intrinsic, ultrafast magnetization fluctuations relevant to high-speed, low-noise spintronic devices. Antiferromagnets are highlighted as promising due to terahertz magnon frequencies, lack of stray fields, and robustness. The authors use femtosecond noise correlation spectroscopy (FemNoC) to measure time-domain correlations of polarization noise linked to out-of-plane spin fluctuations via the Faraday effect. They analyze how temperature and external magnetic field affect the quasi-ferromagnetic (qF) magnon mode and random telegraph noise (RTN) across the spin reorientation transition (SRT), using atomistic spin noise simulations and phenomenological Monte Carlo simulations based on a Landau-type free energy potential. Results show that fluctuation amplitude increases where the free energy potential softens, with qF mode variance enhanced and qF mode frequency softened near the SRT, while an external magnetic field suppresses fluctuations and increases the qF frequency by effectively stiffening the potential. The study concludes that FemNoC reveals a direct relationship between fluctuation amplitude and free energy curvature, and demonstrates tunability of ultrafast spin fluctuations through external control parameters.

The passage describes a camera module and its molded circuit board assembly/photosensitive assembly, using molding technology for mass production. It cites prior “molded packaging” approaches and explains shortcomings for small, precise camera modules, including deformation during demolding, stray-light effects that degrade imaging quality, and unsuitability of certain through-hole and encapsulation shapes for optical performance and manufacturing.  

The invention proposes a molded circuit board assembly in which a molded base is integrally formed on a circuit board and includes a light window (not a prismatic column shape). The molded base has sloped/aslant inner and outer side surfaces defined by multiple acute inclination angles (with specified ranges in embodiments) to reduce friction and damage during demolding, reduce the likelihood of light reaching the photosensitive element, and improve stray-light behavior. The molded base can form a sloped or multi-step-shaped light window to increase light flux while meeting mounting requirements for a lens, lens actuator, optical filter, or filter holder.  

It further describes molded base/window forming blocks in a molding mold, including trapezoidal or multi-step trapezoidal cross-sections with diameters increasing from bottom to top to facilitate demolding. Manufacturing methods are provided for molded circuit board assemblies and molded photosensitive assemblies, including placing boards in a mold, filling liquid molding material into guide grooves while preventing filling at the light window block position, solidifying, and demolding. The passage also outlines molding mold structures, materials, and optional array manufacturing (integral board arrays molded together and later cut).

David Hardt co-lectures on how manufacturing processes can be defined in terms of geometric change and modeled as directed energy exchanges between equipment and material. He discusses a taxonomy for control based on geometry vs. property changes, and serial vs. parallel interaction modes, illustrated with examples such as turning, injection molding, laser processing, CVD, rolling, and machining comparisons. He explains that the location and intensity (and distribution over time or space) of energy determine geometry outcomes, and that different energy modes (mechanical, electrical, thermal, chemical) affect process quality, rate, and side effects through mechanisms like diffusion and repeatability. Hardt provides a framework dividing process influences into equipment/material states and properties, arguing that equipment states are generally more controllable, while material uncertainties are major sources of variation.

The speaker says they are happy to be part of a group, with many players returning from the previous year. They describe the challenge of trying to win back-to-back and say the feeling of overcoming difficulties and sharing it with teammates, family, and friends is what matters. They emphasize the group’s competitive nature, willingness to do whatever it takes, and each player caring about both their own game and their teammates. The speaker highlights contributions from specific players and mentions lineup changes, veteran acquisitions, and strong performances by goaltenders in playoff games. They conclude that winning is difficult, note the joy of seeing a long-time player appreciate the championship, and express happiness about being able to pass the win to him.

The passage discusses the adoption of AI in education and notes that limited quantitative research has assessed administrators’ and college teachers’ views on AI use in secondary and higher education, particularly in the Arab region. It reviews prior studies on teachers’ and students’ perceptions, potential benefits, and concerns such as AI replacing teacher roles, assessment relevance, and challenges to effective AI integration. The passage then presents a cross-sectional study at Kuwait University using an online questionnaire with 63 randomly sampled members of academic staff and administrators. The instruments measured attitudes toward AI, teachers’ perspectives on AI, and scenarios and applications of AI in education. Results show medium acceptance of AI overall (mean 3.37), high consensus that AI will benefit humanity (mean 4.03), and that many participants lacked prior AI teaching experience. The study reports moderate views on linking education to AI (overall mean 4.21), high perceived challenges and difficulties using AI (mean 4.83), and strong agreement on key AI education scenarios such as personalized intelligent teaching and smart schools (overall mean 4.82). Statistically insignificant differences were found by gender, academic degree, and department in most areas, with differences in challenges and difficulties between males and females. The conclusion states that both apprehensions and potentiality are high for AI integration in education and that reforms and technologically aligned pedagogy are needed.

The lecture explains how neutral atoms interact and why this leads to van der Waals forces. Starting from classical physics, the force between neutral atoms is argued to vanish because creating dipole moments costs more energy than is gained from dipole interactions, and the dipole expectation value is zero. Quantum mechanics changes this because the square of the dipole operator is nonzero due to zero-point fluctuations, producing correlated dipole moments and a nonzero average force. The van der Waals potential scales as \(1/R^6\), computed via perturbation theory: for two ground-state atoms the leading term appears in second order, giving a first-order \(1/R^3\) term with a \(C_3\) coefficient only for excited/ground cases, and a second-order \(1/R^6\) term with a \(C_6\) coefficient for two ground states. The lecture also presents alternative pictures: two coupled LC circuits and a mechanism where spontaneous fluctuations stimulate correlated induced dipoles, again yielding \(1/R^6\). It then discusses the role of electromagnetic-field vacuum fluctuations, which can produce a different long-range behavior (Casimir-Polder potential) scaling as \(1/R^7\) when propagation effects matter. Finally, a diagrammatic (QED) approach is described to interpret the interaction as virtual photon exchange between atoms, using perturbation order, intermediate-state energy defects, and the distinction between short-range (where atomic excitation energy is smaller than relevant photon energy) and long-range (where atomic excitation energy dominates).

The lecture introduces risk preferences in economics, focusing first on the expected utility model and later on an alternative reference dependence approach. It discusses how economists assume people are risk averse in many contexts and explains why risk aversion is often modeled through concave utility (diminishing marginal utility of wealth), while noting this approach ignores factors like anxiety and regret. The lecture presents “stylized facts” about risk behavior, including that many people buy insurance and that risk reduction typically has a cost, but people still take risks when expected returns are high. It then defines expected utility, expected monetary value, and formalizes risk neutrality, risk aversion, and risk lovingness. Using examples, it shows how concavity of utility leads risk-averse agents to reject fair gambles. The lecture then explains limitations of expected utility: Rabin’s result implies that if people reject small-scale fair gambles, the model predicts implausibly extreme risk aversion for large-scale choices. To address measurement, it describes risk aversion parameters—absolute and relative risk aversion (including CRRA)—and outlines methods to infer them via certainty equivalents and real-world choice data. As a practical example, it previews Justin Sydnor’s study using home insurance deductible choices to estimate risk aversion (gamma), using the structure of deductibles, premiums, and claim probabilities from a large insurance provider’s data.

Sears is borrowing $100 million from affiliates of CEO Eddie Lampert’s hedge fund, ESL Investments, and ESL Investments also agreed to lend up to an additional $100 million by December 1. Over the last two years, Lampert and his hedge fund have loaned Sears close to $2 billion. Sears plans to close more than 300 Kmart and Sears stores in 2017, reducing its store count to less than 1,140 from 2,073 five years ago. In the second quarter, sales at stores open at least a year fell 11.5%, and total revenue fell 22% to $4.37 billion, mainly due to store closures.

CSUSB veteran students describe tuition benefits for active duty members and veterans, including active duty tuition assistance of up to $4,500 per year on a per-class basis. Danny Sanchez says military training obligations can interrupt school and recommends using the GI Bill after service; he notes the Post-9/11 GI Bill can provide up to four years of education benefits for eligible service members and veterans, who have served at least 90 days on active duty. The Post-9/11 GI Bill allows military members 10–15 years to use benefits after leaving service, with the option to take time off and reapply within that timeframe, and it pays tuition in full for public schools. The Montgomery GI Bill is described as similar but requiring full-time students to pay tuition, fees, books, and other education-related expenses, while Post-9/11 covers those fees. Joseph Patterson and Otis Douglas discuss incentives and plans for further education, including using remaining GI Bill time.

Preparation of numerous memoranda for President Roosevelt and the American delegation for the Malta and Yalta Conferences (Jan. 30–Feb. 11, 1945) was completed on Jan. 16, 1945, and a “Yalta Briefing Book” binder of materials was presented shortly afterward for the President to take to the Three-Power meeting. The passage then describes a memorandum of conversation by Leo Pasvolsky reporting a second meeting with the Soviet Ambassador at the Ambassador’s request to continue discussions of the Dumbarton Oaks proposals, including topics such as a voting formula and other open items (the Court, dependent areas/colonial issues, and international trusteeship), with Pasvolsky outlining various alternative approaches and discussing how related questions might be handled at future conferences or by United Nations bodies.

R. L. Wells was convicted of embezzlement and sentenced to two years in the penitentiary. After his appeal was filed, he entered an appeal bond under article 904 of the Revised C. O. P.; it was properly approved by the sheriff but was not approved by the judge who tried the case (Judge Munroe). Instead, it was approved by Judge Oltorf as special judge. Because article 904 requires the trial judge to approve the bond, the bond was deemed insufficient, and the appeal was dismissed.

An indictment against Alexander Shircliff and Edward O’Connor alleged a conspiracy to bribe and influence a township school trustee to employ O’Connor as a public school teacher, based on sections 2139 and 2009 of the Revised Statutes of 1881. The court held the indictment was not double and that it was sufficient without alleging schools were vacant, since trustees must employ teachers and the conspiracy involved conduct that “might legally come before” the trustee. The court also ruled that issues regarding a continuance and evidentiary rulings were not reviewable because the necessary affidavits and objections were not properly brought into the record by a bill of exceptions. It further held that objections to O’Connor’s discharge as a witness were waived when first raised on appeal. Regarding the appointment of special judges after the appellant absented himself and his bond was forfeited, the court presumed regularity and upheld the validity of the special judge who ultimately rendered judgment. The judgment was affirmed.

Congressional Democrats are opposing a GOP-backed spending proposal as shutdown talks near the funding deadline. House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries said Democrats will not support a partisan Republican spending bill and criticized Republican trustworthiness on health care. Democrats want any deal to extend enhanced Obamacare tax credits due to expire at the end of 2025, while Republicans want negotiations on future extensions after a Senate funding resolution. A government shutdown will occur at 12:01 a.m. Wednesday unless a deal is reached, and President Trump is set to meet at 3 p.m. ET with Jeffries, Chuck Schumer, Mike Johnson, and John Thune. At least seven Senate Democrats would need to vote with Republicans to pass legislation averting a shutdown.

H&M said its March sales growth missed a preliminary estimate, indicating it may struggle to meet its new full-year growth target. Analysts cited a tough market, noting earlier weak performance and that the company faces stiff competition, including from Primark and online players. CEO Karl-Johan Persson said weaker-than-expected first-quarter sales make the full-year 10-15 percent growth goal harder. H&M continues to open many stores despite concerns about the weak clothing market; it had 4,426 stores at end-March, up 11 percent year-on-year. Societe Generale said the company’s main “value fashion” concept is in the most price-competitive segment, while H&M is also investing in higher-priced brands and a more flexible supply chain.

The passage is from Microsoft Corporation’s Form 10‑K for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2022. The Business section describes Microsoft’s mission, key products and services across cloud, productivity, intelligent cloud/edge, and personal computing, and discusses corporate social responsibility initiatives (sustainability, carbon negative goals, racial equity, digital skills) and human capital practices (workforce size, culture, diversity and inclusion, pay equity, wellness and safety, and learning and development). It also outlines Microsoft’s operating segments (Productivity and Business Processes, Intelligent Cloud, and More Personal Computing), major offerings within each segment, distribution and licensing options, customer types, executive officers, available investor information, and begins Item 1A Risk Factors focused on strategic and competitive risks.

The case Leslie B. Canion v. United States (decided October 10, 1958) was submitted for reappraisement based on a stipulation. The parties agreed the merchandise was glassware, furniture, and smoker’s articles exported from France, with the same issues of fact and law as in Bert Friedberg & Co. v. United States. They further stipulated how foreign market value at export was determined, including that it equaled invoice unit values plus 12.44% plus packing (as found by the appraiser), with no higher export value, and that there was an excess of 40 boxes of item number 21008 valued at 337 French francs each plus 12.44% plus packing. The judge found the foreign value under section 402(c) of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended, to be the proper basis and ordered judgment accordingly.

The U.S. government has provided more than $55,000 to Cambodia to preserve personal belongings of prisoners from the Khmer Rouge’s Tuol Sleng (S-21) prison and torture center. A project agreement was signed by U.S. Ambassador William Heidt and Cambodian Secretary of State Chuch Phoeurn. The funding is intended to conserve 3,000 to 5,000 items such as clothing, shoes, hats, and belts, which are deteriorating. The belongings are described as reflecting personal stories of victims, including adults and children, and some items still show stains. Chuch Phoeurn said the preservation can help educate young Cambodians, and some items will be displayed at the Tuol Sleng Genocide Museum.

Connor McDavid signed a two-year, $25 million extension with the Oilers, finalized Monday morning and completed within hours. ESPN also reports the Oilers signed defenseman Jake Walman to a seven-year, $49 million extension starting next season, less than two hours after McDavid’s deal. McDavid, 28, had been set to become an unrestricted free agent after this season and has 1,082 career points. The passage also notes Edmonton is extending coach Knoblauch through 2028-29 and that the extension keeps long-term deals in place for three of the Oilers’ top-six defensemen, including Nurse and Bouchard.

The passage outlines U.S. objectives regarding dependent territories, including promoting self-governance, higher economic and social standards, security safeguards, and non-discriminatory treatment for nationals of peace-loving states. It describes a March 9, 1943 draft declaration that distinguished mandated/detached territories from colonial territories, proposing international trusteeship for the former and progressive self-government leading to full independence for colonial peoples on a fixed time schedule. The draft and related ideas were discussed with the British at Quebec and with the British and Russians at Moscow, with further refinements before the Dumbarton Oaks Conversations and planned submission to the President for approval before broader discussions. It also notes that the chapter on international trusteeship was deleted from American tentative proposals to avoid difficult territorial questions, so dependent territories were not discussed at Dumbarton Oaks despite interest by the British, Soviet, and Chinese governments. The passage then includes Document 5, a letter from Leo Pasvolsky expressing U.S. gratification at alignment with the British government on Security Council voting. Document 6 is a memorandum from Secretary of War Stimson arguing against putting “the cart before the horse,” urging thorough discussion among major powers and caution about raising territorial questions during the war, especially before Russia commits to participation in the Pacific war.

Turing GPUs support real-time ray tracing, but the number of rays per pixel varies with factors such as scene complexity, resolution, other rendered effects, and GPU horsepower. The NVIDIA Real-Time Ray Tracing Denoiser can significantly reduce the number of rays needed per pixel while maintaining high results. The passage describes how ray tracing quality can approach high-end movie and professional non-real-time rendering results, including ray-traced reflections, area light shadows, and ambient occlusion running on GPUs such as Quadro RTX 6000 or GeForce RTX 2080 Ti. It explains that Turing’s hardware ray tracing acceleration is built around RT Cores in each SM, which accelerate BVH traversal and ray/triangle intersection testing, offloading work from the SM and enabling real-time ray tracing. It also compares Turing ray tracing performance to Pascal, introduces NVIDIA NGX (with Turing Tensor Cores) and DLSS, and describes other Turing rendering technologies including Mesh Shading, Variable Rate Shading (VRS), Texture Space Shading (TSS), and Multi-View Rendering (MVR). The text further covers VR-related features (including VRS foveated rendering and VRWorks Audio acceleration), outlines GPU architecture details for TU102/TU104/TU106 and Tesla T4, and presents a workload-based performance metric (RTX-OPS) for hybrid rendering, alongside basic ray tracing mechanics and BVH/denoising concepts.

The passage is a message to Congress submitting a letter from the U.S. agent with the Creek Indians. It states that Georgia surveyors have surveyed lands within Indian Territory protected by a Washington treaty, and that at least one surveyor may have been arrested. It cites the March 30, 1802 act, which penalizes citizens who settle, survey, or mark boundaries on treaty-secured lands, and describes procedures for apprehending violators through either military enforcement or civilian arrest and trial. The Executive decided first to use only civil process: the Secretary of War instructed a U.S. attorney and marshal in Georgia to prosecute the complained-of surveyors, and orders were sent to assure the Indians their treaty rights will be protected and to urge restraint. The passage explains this choice to avoid a conflict with Georgia’s asserted authority and Union-state military collision, while asserting that Georgia’s actions violate the Constitution and the treaty. It concludes that if Georgia persists and federal law remains, the President must enforce federal law even with military force if other means fail, and asks Congress to consider further legislation.
